hero.narrative_lead: Your alderman since 2019. Seven years of receipts, and the work is not finished. A third term for
hero.narrative_run: Byron Sigcho-Lopez is running for a third term as Alderman of the 25th Ward: Pilsen, Little Village, Heart of Chicago, Marshall Square, and University Village. The campaign launched August 18, 2026 in Pilsen.
hero.summary: Over 800 units of affordable housing. Ward Night every Tuesday for seven years, including through the pandemic. Not one dollar from developers or corporate PACs since 2015. This summer the machine's lawyers kept his name off a congressional ballot. The ward is a different story, and on February 23 the neighbors decide it.

promise.label: Promises Kept
promise.headline: He Said He Would. He Did.
promise.beat1: In 2019, the 25th Ward closed a 23 year chapter of Danny Solis and elected a teacher and organizer who took no money from developers. Neighbors have been checking the receipts ever since.
promise.k1_title: Take no developer or corporate money
promise.k1_desc: Not one dollar since 2015. Byron has upheld that commitment every year in office, and he has pushed for publicly financed elections so no alderman has to depend on that money.
promise.k2_desc: Ward Night every Tuesday since 2019, including all the way through the pandemic. Masks and sanitizer delivered door to door. An emergency fund of nearly $100,000 for neighbors who qualified for nothing else, including undocumented neighbors.
promise.k3_title: Put zoning back in the neighbors' hands
promise.k3_desc: A resident Zoning Advisory Board, with members from every neighborhood in the ward, now weighs in on what gets built. In April 2026 that board reviewed Casa Nayarit, the first 76 permanently affordable homes on the Pilsen lot the city bought after Byron blocked 500 luxury apartments.
promise.k4_desc: Over 800 units of affordable housing created or preserved. Over $500,000 from the state for violence prevention. Over $1 million for Benito Juarez and other ward schools. Cermak Road repaved, and 311 pushed until the potholes and the streetlights got fixed.
promise.close: Seven years later the list is longer and the promise has not changed. On February 23, 2027, the 25th Ward decides whether the work keeps going.

bio.label: Meet Byron
bio.headline: Byron Sigcho-Lopez is a father of triplets and the independent socialist alderman who closed a 23 year chapter of machine corruption in the 25th Ward.
bio.p1: Byron is an immigrant who came to the United States alone when he was 17 years old. His life is a testament to what happens when strangers become neighbors and family.
bio.p2: Since 2019 he has delivered for the ward, not for donors. Over 800 units of affordable housing created or preserved. The largest vacant site in Pilsen, at 18th and Peoria, bought by the city after he blocked luxury towers, with Casa Nayarit now selected to build the first 76 permanently affordable homes there. Over $500,000 in state funds for violence prevention. Over $1 million in infrastructure for Benito Juarez Community Academy. Ward Night every Tuesday, including through the pandemic.
bio.p3: He is running for a third term because the work is not finished. Rent stabilization and a property tax system that protects seniors and working families. An elected school board. A reopened Department of the Environment. Street vendors who can work without a misdemeanor arrest turning into a deportation. A ward office that answers to neighbors and not to developers.
bio.p4: Byron earned his Bachelor's in Mathematics and Business Administration from Cumberland University and his Master's in Economics from the University of Illinois at Chicago. He lives in Pilsen with his wife, Loreen, their triplets, a dog, and two cats.
bio.quote_card: "It takes people and people defeats money."

platform.label: The Record
platform.headline: What the 25th Ward built, and what we finish next.

housing.title: Affordable homes you can walk past
housing.desc: Over 800 units of affordable housing created or preserved since 2019. Casa Yucatán tops out at 98 affordable apartments on 21st Place, rents starting at $551, finishing this fall. On the Pilsen lot the city bought for $12 million after Byron blocked 500 luxury apartments, Casa Nayarit will bring 76 permanently affordable homes and a child care center, phase one of 432. He also passed protections for homeowners and seniors against predatory developers.

safety.title: Safety built block by block
safety.desc: When City Hall left violence prevention out of the budget, Byron worked with state and county partners to bring over $500,000 for public safety infrastructure to the ward and $80,000 for programming at Rudy Lozano Alternative High School. Neighbors organized 2532 to reduce gun violence block by block, and the ward office works street by street with residents on the root causes of harm.

schools.title: Strong schools, open libraries, air you can breathe
schools.desc: Over $1 million in state infrastructure for Benito Juarez Community Academy and other 25th Ward schools, and the process started to expand the Rudy Lozano library. Byron joined the hunger strike to #StopGeneralIron, won a commitment to a cumulative burden health impact study, and stood with PERRO demanding toxics testing and dust control before any teardown at the old Fisk power station on Cermak.

accountability.title: Not for sale, and never was
accountability.desc: Byron took disgraced former Alderman Danny Solis all the way to the Illinois Supreme Court to stop campaign cash from paying for a criminal defense lawyer. The court said the election code does not bar it and left the fix to the legislature, so that is where the fight goes next. He does not take contributions from large corporations or developers, and he has upheld that commitment every year in office.

anointment.label: This Summer
anointment.headline: The Ward Is a Different Story
anointment.b1: Byron ran for Congress as an independent this year. Neighbors filed more than double the signatures the law demanded of him, and the machine's lawyers challenged them until an electoral board struck his name from the November ballot.
anointment.b2: He is challenging that rule in federal court, in his words, so our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate. And he is home, running for the ward he has served since 2019.
anointment.kicker: They can object to a petition. They cannot object to a neighbor's ballot.

meet.hero_badge: INDEPENDENT DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST • CHICAGO DSA • 25TH WARD
meet.hero_sub: From Ecuador to Tennessee to Pilsen. Byron Sigcho-Lopez came to this country alone at 17 and has spent his life fighting alongside the working class as a teacher, researcher, organizer, and unapologetic democratic socialist.
meet.hero_thesis: "Justice is not a destination. It is the road that is traveled." This is the road that made Byron.
meet.origin_p1: Byron first came to the United States alone as a teenager, settling in Tennessee and then moving to the Chicago area and Pilsen over 10 years ago. He was born and raised in Quito, Ecuador and came to the US following political instability in the country, and a tragic car accident that left his mother in a coma.
meet.origin_p2: Emergency services were nearly non-existent during this period, and his family's lives were saved by passing motorists who stopped, rescued his family from the wreckage, and drove them to the hospital. When his mother awoke from the coma, she insisted her eldest leave the country for his last year of high school.
meet.origin_p3: When Byron arrived in Tennessee at the age of 17, he knew no one in the country and did not speak English. He was taken in by a generous family who gave him a home and helped him pursue an education.
meet.education_p1: Byron first visited Chicago with his Tennessee family who had loved ones in the Chicago area. During this first trip, they brought Byron to Pilsen to have dinner at the Nuevo Leon restaurant.
meet.education_p2: After graduating high school in Tennessee, Byron was able to attend college on a soccer scholarship after receiving an honorable mention for the All-State Tennessee Soccer Team in high school. Byron graduated from Cumberland University with his Bachelors in Mathematics and Business Administration.
meet.education_p3: He was also awarded the prestigious President's Award for his exceptional academic performance, and many contributions and successes in the school community during his time there. After graduation, Byron returned to Chicago and eventually settled in Pilsen to start his life.
meet.record_desc: Byron became an adult education teacher at the University of Illinois at Chicago and founded the UIC Center for Literacy's Spanish literacy program, making the GED program at UIC much more widely accessible to Spanish speaking immigrants and residents. Seeing the need for wrap-around services, Byron also brought a case worker into the program to ensure his students' families received resources and needed services.
meet.record_desc2: In addition to Byron's work as a teacher, he also volunteered as a youth soccer coach at Pilsen Academy. Byron earned a Master's Degree in Economics from UIC while also working as a lead researcher. He began collaborating alongside the Chicago Teachers Union in investigating the financial relationships between charter school networks like UNO, school funding, and Chicago's political elite, and organized with parents and teachers like Karen Lewis to fight for fully funded public schools.
meet.schools_desc: After Rahm Emanuel announced that he would be closing a hundred thirty Chicago Public Schools, Byron became involved in the Pilsen Alliance where he organized with the community to push to keep the schools open.
meet.first_run_desc: In 2015, Byron was encouraged by community leaders Nellie Cotton and Kit Duffy to run for Alderman against the machine - now disgraced former Alderman Danny Solis. Byron came in second in the 5-way race.
meet.alliance_desc: Byron eventually served as the Director of Pilsen Alliance where he became a leader and an activist in the fight against gentrification, displacement, and corruption.
meet.dsa_desc: He joined forces with organizers from the Chicago Democratic Socialists of America while partnering on the coalition to Lift the Ban on Rent Control across the state of Illinois, and became a member then and there.
meet.elected_headline: A Grassroots Movement, Not a Machine Candidacy
meet.elected_p1: In 2019, Byron ran a grassroots campaign for Alderman of the 25th Ward. He committed to refuse political contributions from developers and big corporations - a commitment he has upheld to this day and beyond. Since taking office, any resident now can personally meet with Byron at his weekly Ward Night, and all residents can receive compassion, support, and city services from the devoted public servants who staff the 25th Ward office.
meet.elected_p2: In 2023, big money and the political establishment lined up against Byron. Byron took democratic establishment and corrupt Danny Solis all the way to the Illinois Supreme Court over his unethical campaign finance practices. The voters of the 25th Ward sent him back to City Hall.
meet.elected_2026: In 2026, Byron ran for Congress as an independent, and the machine's lawyers worked to keep his name off the ballot. He came home to run for a third term, back to stand with the 25th Ward that raised him up.
meet.elected_p3: As an elected official, he used the power of his office to put the people's power into the institutions that needed it - under his leadership, change is happening.
meet.achieve_housing_desc: Byron has preserved and created over 800 units of affordable housing across Chicago and as Chairman of the Committee on Housing and Real Estate, made Chicago the largest city to pass a $135 million dollar investment via the Green Social Housing Initiative, to build sustainable housing and help address the housing crisis in Illinois.
meet.achieve_wardnight_desc: Every community member has the opportunity to speak directly with their elected official every Tuesday at the Ward Office - the accountability is a commitment.
meet.achieve_health_desc: The Pilsen Food Pantry has grown to serve more than ever. Perpetrators of heinous crimes are held accountable more often and public safety has become more possible for the community to organize for. A dental clinic accessible to the people was opened and a mental health clinic as well.
meet.achieve_fight_desc: Property tax payers know that their elected official has voted against every single proposed property tax increase, and worked to fight for a statewide millionaire surcharge and wealth taxes on the billionaires. When Trump sent ICE to our communities, Byron faced them head on with the full weight of his office and his community ensuring that Bovino and other thugs were held accountable to the furthest extent possible in court.
meet.elected_call: Byron has changed what was possible in public service on the municipal level and he isn't stopping. We need him back at City Hall for the 25th Ward.
meet.family_desc: Byron, and his wife Loreen, live in Pilsen with their little triplets (who attend public school), and their dog, Buster, and their two cats Dos and 三歲.
meet.caption_ecuador: Byron with his family in Quito, Ecuador
meet.caption_cumberland: Receiving the President's Award at Cumberland University
meet.caption_schools: Fighting for investment in our neighborhood schools

issues.hero_headline: Not Promises. Receipts. Seven Years Delivering for the 25th Ward.
issues.hero_sub: In 2019, Byron Sigcho-Lopez took the 25th Ward from a 23-year machine and never took a dime from it. This is what he delivered as your Alderman, and what he is fighting for next.
issues.another_world: Another world is not only possible. It is necessary.
issues.another_world_sub: In the 25th Ward, we are already building it.
issues.public_safety_title: Public safety, built block by block
issues.public_safety_desc: When City Hall left violence prevention out of the budget, Byron went around it. He brought more than $500,000 in state funding for public safety infrastructure into the ward, plus $80,000 for programming at Rudy Lozano Alternative High School.
issues.public_safety_desc2: Out of his regular community safety meetings, neighbors built 2532, a resident-led organization that applies block-by-block strategies to reduce gun violence and address its root causes across the 25th Ward.
issues.public_safety_desc3: He has pushed the Chicago Police Department for accountability on low clearance rates, worked with victims of violence and their families to get answers, and backed residents and business owners raising concerns on their own blocks.
issues.housing_caption: Listening to neighbors, door to door
issues.housing_title: 800 units delivered. Two more rising now.
issues.housing_desc: The Chicago Tribune's 2023 endorsement credits Byron with enabling the creation and preservation of more than 800 affordable units in the ward, many of them family-sized. In April 2026, the city selected The Resurrection Project to build Casa Nayarit, 76 permanently affordable homes plus a child care center at 900 W. 18th St., the first building on the lot at 18th and Peoria that the city bought for $12 million after Byron blocked a developer's plan for 500 luxury apartments there. It is phase one of 432 units planned for the six-acre site, and the resident-led Zoning Advisory Board reviewed the project in April 2026 before it moved forward.
issues.housing_desc2: A few blocks away, Casa Yucatán, 98 affordable apartments at 1609 W. 21st Place with rents starting at $551, topped out in March 2026 and is set to finish this fall. Byron also co-chaired the mayor's Affordable Requirements Ordinance task force, helped double the ARO minimum from 10% to 20%, and passed legislation protecting homeowners, seniors, and longtime residents from harassment by predatory developers.
issues.housing_desc3: The 2022 reassessment took 46 percent from Pilsen homeowners overnight. The next citywide reassessment lands in 2027, and Byron has voted against every proposed property tax increase, while his ward office helps neighbors sign up for the property tax exemptions they are owed right now.
issues.schools_title: Every school funded, every library open
issues.schools_desc: As a teacher himself, Byron knows what our schools and libraries mean to the strength of this community. He worked with the State of Illinois to secure more than $1 million in infrastructure improvements at Benito Juarez Community Academy and other 25th Ward public schools, and he initiated the long-overdue expansion of the Rudy Lozano Public Library.
issues.schools_desc2: He stood against retaliation targeting teachers, including a 25th Ward resident, after they joined the fight against environmental racism during the General Iron hunger strike. He is fighting for fully funded public schools and an elected school board now.
issues.environment_caption: Raising his voice for environmental justice
issues.environment_desc: Byron and PERRO, the Pilsen Environmental Rights and Reform Organization, are demanding toxics testing, remediation, and a real dust-control plan before Midwest Generation tears down the century-old Fisk power station at 1111 W. Cermak Rd. In October 2025 he threatened to block the demolition outright. Every neighbor in Pilsen and Little Village remembers the 2020 Hilco implosion at the old Crawford plant, and he is making sure it does not happen twice.
issues.environment_desc2: He is pushing the same accountability into the Pilsen industrial corridor, where neighbors are demanding the city add green space and shut down the corridor's biggest polluters, including Sims Metal Management. This is not new ground for him: he joined the hunger strike that helped stop General Iron from relocating its pollution into a working-class community, won a commitment to a cumulative burden health impact study, and pushed environmental justice criteria into every city procurement contract after holding polluters like MAT Asphalt accountable elsewhere in Chicago.
issues.environment_desc3: Now he is fighting to reopen the Department of the Environment so climate and environmental justice concerns are handled by the city, not left to chance.
issues.gender_equity_title: Reproductive justice and a ward office that leads
issues.gender_equity_desc: Byron pushed the Mayor's Office, alongside his colleagues, to increase funding for LGBTQIA+ inclusive social and health services, and supported legislation making Chicago a reproductive health sanctuary city.
issues.gender_equity_desc2: He is proud to lead the first 25th Ward office with a majority-female leadership team, including his Chief of Staff.
issues.constituent_services_desc: Every Tuesday night, for seven years, including through the pandemic, Byron has hosted Ward Night so residents and stakeholders can bring their concerns to him directly. During the pandemic, he and his team personally delivered masks, sanitizer, and safety supplies across the ward, and his office built an emergency fund of nearly $100,000 for residents who did not qualify for other assistance, including undocumented neighbors.
issues.constituent_services_desc2: The ward office runs MENU participatory budgeting so residents decide how infrastructure dollars get spent, organizes Clean-Up Saturdays every spring and summer, and holds a standing TIF Review Committee open to the public. His team pushes 311 to fill potholes and fix streetlights, led the repaving of Cermak Road, and every winter his office and volunteers shovel for elderly and disabled residents.
issues.economic_caption: On the picket line with striking workers
issues.economic_title: Standing with workers and small businesses
issues.economic_desc: Byron supported the creation of the Pilsen Chamber of Commerce so small businesses have direct, self-determined access to resources and advocacy, and he is working to integrate the Pilsen and Little Village chambers so the whole ward benefits. When an Amazon distribution facility in the ward failed workers on bathroom access and air conditioning, his office moved fast to win changes.
issues.economic_desc2: He walked the line with unionized and organizing workers across the city, stood with the small businesses of the Little Village Discount Mall through their fight to stay on 26th Street, helped the Pilsen Food Pantry move into a larger space where it now feeds more than 1,500 neighbors a month, and fought to get small businesses reimbursed for license fees they paid but couldn't use during the COVID shutdowns.
issues.economic_desc3: The fight continues. In 2026, street vendors have been caught between CPD misdemeanor arrests and ICE agents waiting at their court hearings, with vendors deported straight out of the courthouse. Byron is fighting for licensing help and legal defense so no one in the 25th Ward is punished with deportation for selling food on a sidewalk.
issues.transparency_title: He took Solis all the way to the Supreme Court
issues.transparency_desc: Byron took disgraced former Alderman Danny Solis all the way to the Illinois Supreme Court over Solis spending $220,000 in campaign funds on his own criminal defense lawyers. In a ward whose last alderman wore a wire for the FBI, the fight itself is the point. Byron has also strengthened the Office of Inspector General as it exposed the Hilco implosion, the illegal raid on Anjanette Young, and public safety failures in our communities.
issues.transparency_desc2: Byron has never taken a dime of corporate or developer money since 2015, and he never will. He is fighting for publicly financed elections, a LaSalle Street tax on the more than a quadrillion dollars in financial transactions that pass through the Chicago Mercantile Exchange tax-free every year, and a public bank so our small businesses and residents can access credit on fair terms.
issues.transparency_desc3: In 2026, when that same political establishment used the courts to strike his name from the congressional ballot, Byron didn't stop fighting. He took Illinois's ballot-access laws to federal court, in his words, so our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate.
issues.unbought_text: Byron completely rejects corporate PAC money and contributions from large real estate developers, a commitment he has kept since 2015. He only answers to the working-class coalition of the 25th Ward. His campaign is funded by small-dollar donations from neighbors, teachers, union members, and working families. This is what it means to be truly independent.
issues.unbought_press_quote: "Lopez has admirably represented his ward in his first term... Lopez is endorsed."
issues.unbought_kicker: "It takes people and people defeats money."

machine.hero_sub: Every ward answers one question: who does your alderman work for, the neighbors or the machine? For 23 years the answer here was the machine. In 2019 the ward took itself back, and it has not been for sale since. On February 23, 2027, we answer again.
machine.movement_intro: Byron Sigcho-Lopez is an ideologically committed democratic socialist and a firebrand who has spent his entire career fighting for the multiracial working class. He is not a politician looking for a promotion. He is an organizer who was called to serve by his community.
machine.unbought_text: Unlike establishment politicians, Byron completely rejects corporate PAC money and contributions from real estate developers. His campaign is powered entirely by thousands of small-dollar grassroots donations from teachers, nurses, union members, and working families. He has upheld this commitment since his first campaign in 2015 and has never wavered.
machine.tested_text: Byron's unique power comes from bottom-up organizing. As 25th Ward Alderperson, he passed anti-displacement legislation to protect homeowners from predatory developers, created over 800 units of affordable housing, stood uncompromisingly with the Chicago Teachers Union, doubled the Affordable Requirements Ordinance minimum, and joined a hunger strike to fight environmental racism. These are not campaign promises. These are receipts.
machine.pullquote: "I have never taken a dollar from a corporation or a developer. I never will. My loyalty is to the people of this district, not to the machine."
machine.thesis: "Democracy cannot be preserved nationally if it is subverted locally."
machine.timeline_intro: A machine ward is not held by good work. It is held by four habits, and the 25th Ward lived under all of them.
machine.pattern_1: Campaign accounts filled by developers and corporate PACs, so the votes at City Hall answer to the people who wrote the checks instead of the people on the block.
machine.pattern_2: One alderman deciding what gets built, behind a closed door, with neighbors told after the permits are already pulled.
machine.pattern_3: The Chicago Tribune reported in 2023 that Danny Solis spent $220,000 from his campaign fund on criminal defense lawyers during the federal probe at City Hall. Byron took it all the way to the Illinois Supreme Court, which condemned the corruption and ruled that only the legislature can ban the practice.
machine.pattern_4: And when the votes are not there, the lawyers are. This summer their objections kept Byron's name off a congressional ballot. A ward is a different story: here they have to beat him in front of the neighbors.
machine.cta_headline: This Ward Is Not For Sale. Let's Keep It That Way.

volunteer.hero_headline: We Know How to Knock On Doors. Now We Do It for the Ward.
volunteer.hero_sub: We don't have corporate PAC money or backroom bosses. We have you. Join the multiracial working-class coalition that keeps the 25th Ward unbought and re-elects Byron Sigcho-Lopez.
volunteer.hero_status: THE WARD CAMPAIGN BEGINS. ELECTION DAY: FEBRUARY 23, 2027.
volunteer.blitz_p1: This summer, machine lawyers kept his name off a congressional ballot. The 25th Ward tells a different story: we knock every door and answer at the ballot box on February 23, 2027.
volunteer.picker_sub: Don't turn on each other. Uplift each other. Help each other. Show solidarity. Pick what sounds like you and we'll point you to your post.
volunteer.picker_hint: Pick one or more. We'll check the boxes for you below.
volunteer.canvass_desc: Knock on doors in Pilsen, Little Village, Heart of Chicago, and the rest of the 25th Ward for real conversations about housing, safety, and city services. This is how a ground game gets built: block by block, door by door.
volunteer.events_desc: Every Tuesday is Ward Night: neighbors bring their questions straight to Byron's team. Help staff Ward Night, table at block parties and community events, and put a face to this campaign at the places where the ward already gathers.
volunteer.digital_desc: Reach voters where they are through rapid-response text campaigns, phone calls, and social media. This work can be done from anywhere, anytime, and is critical for expanding the movement beyond what door-knocking alone can achieve.
volunteer.precinct_desc: Lead the ground game in your neighborhood. Precinct captains coordinate local volunteers, organize neighbors to re-elect Byron on February 23, 2027, and serve as the backbone of the campaign at the block level. Not selected? Support your captain however you can.
volunteer.creative_desc: Design flyers, create campaign videos, and push content across social media. From graphic design to videography and video editing, your creative skills can amplify Byron's message to thousands of voters.
volunteer.campus_desc: High school ambassadors and college campus captains help mobilize the next generation. Organize voter registration drives, host campus events, and build a youth coalition that fights for affordable education and a livable future.
volunteer.signup_desc: Fill out the form and our team will reach out with next steps. Whether you have one hour or one hundred, there is a role for you in this movement.

duel.r1_machine_text: For 23 years the 25th Ward belonged to Danny Solis and the machine behind him. Zoning, permits, and favors all ran through one office. It ended with the alderman disgraced and a federal investigation working its way through City Hall.
duel.r1_movement_text: When the city moved to close 130 public schools, Byron organized with parents and teachers to keep them open. He went on to lead the Pilsen Alliance, fighting displacement and corruption block by block, years before he ran for anything.
duel.r1_movement_quote: "I do not build coalitions with politicians. I build coalition with my constituents."
duel.r2_machine_text: A machine ward runs on other people's checks. Developers and corporate PACs pay for the campaign, and then the votes follow the money instead of the block.
duel.r2_movement_text: Byron pledged in his first run to refuse contributions from developers and big corporations, and he has kept that pledge through every campaign since. This one is powered by small-dollar donations from teachers, nurses, union members, and working families.
duel.r2_movement_quote: "It takes people and people defeats money."
duel.r3_machine_text: In 2018 Danny Solis rezoned the largest vacant lot in Pilsen from residential to industrial, and the developer pushed for 500 market-rate apartments on it. That is how zoning worked here: one alderman, one closed door, and the block finds out when the permits are pulled.
duel.r3_machine_text2: City Hall also floated landmarking roughly 900 Pilsen homes and buildings, a repair bill long-time owners could not carry.
duel.r3_movement_text: Byron fought the luxury plan as a Pilsen Alliance organizer and blocked it again in 2019 as alderman. The city bought the six-acre lot for $12 million in 2022. In April 2026 Casa Nayarit was selected for it: 76 permanently affordable homes and a ground-floor child care center at 900 W. 18th St, phase one of 432 units, reviewed by the ward's resident zoning advisory board before it moved.
duel.r3_movement_text2: Down the street, Casa Yucatán finishes this fall at 1609 W. 21st Place: 98 affordable apartments. Over 800 affordable units created or preserved since 2019, hundreds of neighbors stopped the landmark plan, and homeowners won real protection from predatory developers.
duel.r4_machine_text: The Chicago Tribune reported in 2023 that Danny Solis spent $220,000 from his campaign fund on criminal defense lawyers during the federal probe at City Hall. Donors gave to a ward. The money went to his lawyers.
duel.r4_stat_defense: campaign funds spent on his defense
duel.r4_movement_title: All the Way to the Supreme Court
duel.r4_movement_text: Byron challenged it and took Danny Solis all the way to the Illinois Supreme Court. In March 2022 the court condemned public corruption in strong terms and still ruled against him: the election code does not ban the practice, and only the legislature can change that. Nobody else in Chicago even tried.
duel.r4_movement_quote: "If the law allows corrupt politicians to use campaign funds for legal defense fees, then it's time to change the law."
duel.r5_machine_text: In the 2023 ward race the business-backed Get Stuff Done PAC dropped just under $160,000 into ads and mailers against Byron and for his challenger, according to Crain's Chicago Business. WTTW reported that nearly 20 percent of the more than $618,000 the PAC spent citywide went to opposing him. Its funders included a financier who has long backed and advised Rahm Emanuel.
duel.r5_movement_text: The answer was doors, Ward Night, and four years of neighbors who knew the office was theirs. The Chicago Tribune endorsed him, writing that he had admirably represented his ward. Gazette Chicago called him the best alderman in the City of Chicago. The ward re-elected him.
duel.r5_movement_quote: "He's the real deal." Girl, I Guess Progressive Voter Guide, 2023.
duel.r6_machine_text: In 2026 the machine handed a Congressional seat to a former chief of staff in the final hours before the deadline, and Byron ran as an independent. She needed 697 signatures. The law demanded 10,816 of him. The movement filed 22,788.
duel.r6_machine_text2: Their lawyers challenged the petitions line by line, and in July 2026 the State Officers Electoral Board voted unanimously to strike him from the November ballot, 1,222 short.
duel.r6_movement_text: Byron sued the Illinois State Board of Elections in federal court. His attorneys told him reinstatement was unlikely. He filed anyway, for whoever runs next.
duel.r6_movement_text2: Then he came home. Byron is running for a third term as Alderman of the 25th Ward, the ward the machine lost in 2019 and has never taken back. Round one went to their lawyers. Round two is February 23, 2027, where objections do not count and voters do.
duel.r6_movement_quote: "This is being done so our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate."

timeline.label: The Long Road
timeline.headline: The Road to February 23
timeline.sigwall_label: signatures filed by volunteers. Every mark is a neighbor.
timeline.s1_desc: The 25th Ward belongs to Danny Solis and the machine behind him. Zoning, permits, and favors run through one office, and it ends with the alderman disgraced and a federal investigation at City Hall.
timeline.s2_desc: The city moves to close 130 public schools. Byron organizes with parents and teachers to keep them open, then leads the Pilsen Alliance against displacement and corruption.
timeline.s3_desc: Byron runs for alderman against Danny Solis and finishes second. He makes a pledge that outlasts the race: no money from developers or big corporations.
timeline.s4_desc: A grassroots campaign wins the 25th Ward, the machine's oldest prize. Ward Night starts every Tuesday, and the doors of the ward office open to everyone.
timeline.s5_desc: 800+ affordable units created or preserved. Zoning opened to residents through the Zoning Advisory Board. $1M+ in state infrastructure for Benito Juarez and ward schools. $500,000+ for violence prevention.
timeline.s6_desc: Crain's reports that the business-backed Get Stuff Done PAC drops just under $160,000 into the ward against Byron, part of more than $618,000 spent citywide, with nearly a fifth of it aimed at him (WTTW). The ward sends Byron back.
timeline.s7_desc: Byron runs for Congress as an independent after the seat is handed to a former chief of staff. She needs 697 signatures. The law demands 10,816 of him. The movement files 22,788, and in July an electoral board strikes him from the November ballot, 1,222 short. He sues in federal court.
timeline.s8_desc: August 18: the movement packs Indígó MRKTŌ in Pilsen to launch the re-election campaign. Byron runs for a third term as Alderman of the 25th Ward, and petition season starts this fall.
timeline.s9_desc: Not the machine. Not their lawyers. The ward decides who its alderman answers to. You decide.
